headline: The packaging regulation applies directly to the food and beverage industry, not just the companies that make packaging.
body: 36 of the packaging regulation's measures name the food and beverage sector directly. The chemicals industry, by contrast, is affected only as a supplier to the companies that make packaging.

evidence.notes: Counts are taken across every row in data/ppwr.json (89 rows). foodbev appears in sectors_named on 36 rows and in sectors_reached on a further 32; the two sets do not overlap, so 68 of the file's 89 rows carry the sector one way or the other. The 36 named rows are FREE-01, FREE-03, SUB-04, REC-04, RCY-01, RCY-02, CMP-01, MIN-01, MIN-02, REU-01, LAB-01, LAB-02, LAB-03, LAB-04, LAB-06, OPS-04, OPS-07, EXC-01, EXC-02, BAN-01, RSY-01, RSY-02, RTG-01, RTG-02, RTG-03, RTG-04, RTG-05, RTG-08, RTG-09, REG-01, REG-02, EPR-01, EPR-04, EPR-05, EPR-06 and INF-01. The five cited rows are drawn from that set: FREE-01 is the market-access gate, MIN-01 the minimisation duty, BAN-01 the Annex V format prohibitions, RCY-01 the recycled-content minimums and EPR-01 the extended-producer-responsibility duty, which addresses producers of packaged products rather than of packaging. The chemicals comparison is the supply route: chem is named on 3 rows and reached on 5, and the stored FIGARO figure has C20 (chemicals) supplying 21.6% of chem/plastics inputs in the EU view. This finding replaces the withdrawn chemicals-led one, which led on that supplier share and did not state the sector the regulation names most often after the packaging makers themselves.
